items.stem: Explain why Castro moved closer to the Soviet Union in 1960–1961.
items.answer: US hostility to land reform and nationalisation, the US sugar quota cut and embargo, and the Bay of Pigs invasion pushed Cuba to seek Soviet trade and protection, consistent with Castro’s radical aims.

items.stem: A student claims that Castro’s regime relied only on repression. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: It also won support through land reform, literacy, free health care and nationalism, alongside the repression of opponents.
items.markingKey: It also won support through land reform, literacy, free health care and nationalism, alongside the repression of opponents. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Omar writes: "Castro came to power as an openly communist leader." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: In 1959 Castro presented himself as a nationalist reformer; he declared the revolution socialist only in April 1961, and the PSP communists initially distrusted him.
items.markingKey: In 1959 Castro presented himself as a nationalist reformer; he declared the revolution socialist only in April 1961, and the PSP communists initially distrusted him. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With reference to the Padilla affair of 1971, explain how it illustrates the control of culture in Castro’s Cuba.
items.answer: The poet Heberto Padilla was arrested and forced to make a public self-criticism, alienating many foreign intellectuals. It demonstrated the limits of artistic freedom set out in “Words to the Intellectuals”.
items.markingKey: Context (The poet Heberto Padilla was arrested and forced to make a public self-criticism, alienating many foreign intellectuals.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that Castro maintained power in Cuba mainly through popular social reforms.
items.answer: Social reform built genuine support, but surveillance, repression and Soviet aid were also essential.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: literacy campaign and free health care; land reform; nationalism and anti-US feeling. Arguments against: CDRs and repression of opponents; emigration of opponents (Mariel); Soviet economic support until 1991. Supported judgement: Social reform built genuine support, but surveillance, repression and Soviet aid were also essential.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "26 July Movement"?
options: Hans Mommsen’s term for the process by which competition within the Nazi state pushed policies towards ever more extreme measures
The interpretation that Hitler’s long-held ideological intentions and personal decisions drove Nazi policy, including the Holocaust
Castro’s revolutionary movement, named after the failed attack on the Moncada barracks on 26 July 1953
Friedrich and Brzezinski’s six features of totalitarian states: an official ideology, a single mass party, terror, a monopoly of communications, a monopoly of weapons and a centrally directed economy
items.answer: Castro’s revolutionary movement, named after the failed attack on the Moncada barracks on 26 July 1953
items.markingKey: C. "26 July Movement" is Castro’s revolutionary movement, named after the failed attack on the Moncada barracks on 26 July 1953.

items.answer: Social reform built genuine support, but surveillance, repression and Soviet aid were also essential.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: literacy campaign and free health care; land reform; nationalism and anti-US feeling. Arguments against: CDRs and repression of opponents; emigration of opponents (Mariel); Soviet economic support until 1991. Supported judgement: Social reform built genuine support, but surveillance, repression and Soviet aid were also essential. Markbands: Use the IB Paper 2/3 markbands, scaled to the marks: top band – clearly focused, well structured, accurate and relevant knowledge used to support critical analysis, different perspectives evaluated, reasoned conclusion; middle band – mostly accurate knowledge, some analysis but partly narrative; lower band – little understanding of the demands, mainly description.

items.stem:
Source A: Paraphrased from Carl J. Friedrich and Zbigniew Brzezinski, US political scientists, Totalitarian Dictatorship and Autocracy, 1956

The totalitarian dictatorships all share six features: an official ideology, a single mass party led by one man, a system of terror, a monopoly of mass communications, a monopoly of weapons, and central control of the economy.

Source B: Paraphrased from Ian Kershaw and Moshe Lewin (eds), Stalinism and Nazism: Dictatorships in Comparison, 1997

Comparing Hitler and Stalin shows as many differences as similarities. Stalin’s regime rested on a bureaucratic party apparatus; Hitler’s was a chaotic personal rule in which party and state agencies competed, held together by the Führer’s charisma.

In what ways do Sources A and B agree and disagree about comparisons between authoritarian states in different regions?
items.answer: Both compare authoritarian regimes. Friedrich and Brzezinski stress shared features of totalitarian control, while Kershaw and Lewin emphasise structural differences between the Nazi and Soviet systems; A generalises, B differentiates.
items.markingKey: Both compare authoritarian regimes. Friedrich and Brzezinski stress shared features of totalitarian control, while Kershaw and Lewin emphasise structural differences between the Nazi and Soviet systems; A generalises, B differentiates. Award 1 mark per valid, explicitly linked point of comparison or contrast, up to [6]; at least one comparison and one contrast are needed for full marks. A running (integrated) comparison is preferred to end-on description; do not credit points about provenance in this question.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The interpretation that Hitler’s long-held ideological intentions and personal decisions drove Nazi policy, including the Holocaust"?
options: Committees for the Defence of the Revolution (CDRs)
items.answer: intentionalism
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of intentionalism.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Castro’s revolutionary movement, named after the failed attack on the Moncada barracks on 26 July 1953"?
options: Committees for the Defence of the Revolution (CDRs)
items.answer: 26 July Movement
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of 26 July Movement.

items.stem: A student claims that comparison means describing two regimes one after the other. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Effective comparison analyses similarities and differences point by point, explaining why they existed.
items.markingKey: Effective comparison analyses similarities and differences point by point, explaining why they existed. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims that the intentionalist–structuralist debate is about whether the Holocaust happened. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Both schools fully accept the Holocaust; they disagree about how and why decisions were made.
items.markingKey: Both schools fully accept the Holocaust; they disagree about how and why decisions were made. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why the CDRs were important in consolidating Castro’s rule.
items.answer: They mobilised hundreds of thousands to monitor neighbours, distribute rations and organise campaigns, extending surveillance and participation into every street.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They mobilised hundreds of thousands to monitor neighbours, distribute rations and organise campaigns, extending surveillance and participation into every street. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between the social base of Maoism and the social base of Nazism.
items.answer: Nazism drew much support from the middle classes, farmers and Protestant voters in an industrial society; Maoism drew its strength from the peasantry in an agrarian society.
items.markingKey: Nazism drew much support from the middle classes, farmers and Protestant voters in an industrial society; Maoism drew its strength from the peasantry in an agrarian society. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Structuralist historians argue that Hitler was unimportant." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Structuralists accept that Hitler’s ideology and authority were essential but argue that decisions emerged from the system rather than detailed plans.
items.markingKey: Structuralists accept that Hitler’s ideology and authority were essential but argue that decisions emerged from the system rather than detailed plans. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Source A: Fidel Castro, closing words of his defence speech at his trial for the Moncada attack, Santiago de Cuba, 16 October 1953 (extract; the speech was later rewritten and published as a pamphlet)

I know that imprisonment will be harder for me than it has ever been for anyone. But I do not fear prison, as I do not fear the fury of the miserable tyrant who took the lives of my comrades. Condemn me. It does not matter. History will absolve me.

Evaluate Source A as evidence about the emergence and rule of Fidel Castro in Cuba, considering its author, date, intended audience and content.
items.answer: Value: It shows Castro’s early self-presentation and the programme he used to build support after Moncada. Limitations: The published version was reconstructed later in prison and used as propaganda, so it may differ from what he said at the trial.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Hitler’s Reichstag speech of 30 January 1939 shows the intentionalist argument.
items.answer: Hitler “prophesied” that a new world war would result in “the annihilation of the Jewish race in Europe”. Intentionalists see it as evidence of a long-held aim; structuralists see it as rhetoric that became policy only in wartime conditions.
items.markingKey: Context (Hitler “prophesied” that a new world war would result in “the annihilation of the Jewish race in Europe”.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Intentionalists see it as evidence of a long-held aim; structuralists see it as rhetoric that became policy only in wartime conditions. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the intentionalist argument.

items.stem: Briefly describe the literacy campaign of 1961 and explain what it reveals about the use of social policy to build support.
items.answer: About 250,000 volunteers, including 100,000 young brigadistas, taught over 700,000 people to read; literacy rose to about 96%. It improved lives and mobilised youth for the revolution, while spreading revolutionary ideology.
items.markingKey: Context (About 250,000 volunteers, including 100,000 young brigadistas, taught over 700,000 people to read; literacy rose to about 96%.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: It improved lives and mobilised youth for the revolution, while spreading revolutionary ideology. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the use of social policy to build support.

Comparing Hitler and Stalin shows as many differences as similarities. Stalin’s regime rested on a bureaucratic party apparatus; Hitler’s was a chaotic personal rule in which party and state agencies competed, held together by the Führer’s charisma.

Explain the view of comparisons between authoritarian states in different regions that is presented in Source B.
items.answer: Nazi and Soviet regimes differed significantly in structure: bureaucratic party rule versus chaotic charismatic rule.

items.stem:
Source A: Paraphrased from Lucy Dawidowicz, US historian, The War Against the Jews, 1933–1945, 1975

The Final Solution grew out of Hitler’s ideas; it was his intention from the start. He had laid out his programme in Mein Kampf, and he carried it out when war gave him the opportunity.

Source B: Werner Willikens, State Secretary in the Prussian Ministry of Agriculture, speech to officials, 21 February 1934 (extract, translation)

It is the duty of everybody to try to work towards the Führer along the lines he would wish. Whoever works correctly towards the Führer along his lines and towards his goal will in future have the finest reward.

To what extent do Sources A and B present a similar picture of the intentionalist–structuralist debate on the Nazi state and the Holocaust?
items.answer: Both place Hitler at the centre of policy. Dawidowicz argues that Hitler planned the Holocaust from the start, whereas Willikens shows officials acting on Hitler’s presumed wishes rather than specific orders; A suggests a top-down plan, B a system of anticipation from below.
items.markingKey: Both place Hitler at the centre of policy. I know that imprisonment will be harder for me than it has ever been for anyone. But I do not fear prison, as I do not fear the fury of the miserable tyrant who took the lives of my comrades. Condemn me. It does not matter. History will absolve me.

Source B: Fidel Castro, “Words to the Intellectuals”, speech at the National Library, Havana, June 1961 (extract, translation)

Within the Revolution, everything; against the Revolution, nothing. The Revolution has rights too, and the first right of the Revolution is to exist.

Compare and contrast what Sources A and B reveal about the emergence and rule of Fidel Castro in Cuba.
items.answer: Both show Castro presenting the revolution as morally justified. In 1953 he presents himself as a victim appealing to history against tyranny, whereas in 1961 he speaks as the leader of a state setting limits on freedom; A defends rebellion, B restricts dissent.

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of the argument that the similarities between authoritarian states are more significant than their differences.
items.answer: Methods were similar, but differences in ideology, aims and outcomes are historically more significant.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: single party, leader cult, propaganda and terror in all; control of youth and media; crisis conditions for emergence; different ideologies and social bases; scale of terror varied greatly; different relations with traditional elites and churches. A strong answer reaches a judgement such as: Methods were similar, but differences in ideology, aims and outcomes are historically more significant.
